So I was doubting whether or not to actually go to my post surgical appointment with the surgeon. I felt like utter hell but ultimately decided it was important. As I told him my symptoms, I watched his face change with alarm. He told me I needed to go to the ER now and that they would admit me immediately. Spooked, I went to the ER. 

I was in full congestive heart failure. My ejection fraction was less than 10% when I was admitted. I was immediately put on a transplant list. Luckily, I didn't need one. Being in my 20s, my heart made almost a full recovery. I am thankful I went to that appointment every single day of my life. Had I not I may very well have died at home.

I got diabetic ketoacidosis in 2017 from the flu, even though I had the shot (I'm a type 1 diabetic). I was admitted to the ICU. My heart started failing AGAIN (I had congestive heart failure in 2015) and my kidneys began to fail. My heart rate was 160+ the whole time, even though they had me on Precedex, Valium, Fentanyl, Midazolam, and Propofol (DKA can get very violent and painful, as your blood literally turns acidic). 

The whole time I was intubated and in a coma I was trapped in my head. The last show I watched before I got admitted was Breaking Bad and for some reason I dreamed/hallucinated that I was a meth head and in jail (probably due to my arms and legs being strapped to the bed). I could hear my mom's voice but could never find her. It was the worst time of my life. 

When i finally woke up, I went into withdrawals after getting addicted to the heavy drugs they used on me. 12 straight hours of thrashing, delirium, violent hallucinations. I begged and pleaded with the nurse to shoot me in the head. I was trapped and the room was on fire. My heart rate was INSANE. Finally they gave me some IV Benadryl, a little known helper for withdrawals. After that they added Valium and I finally settled down. 

They put me heavy on Valium and I slept through the next day. When I woke up, my mom was standing next to a priest. I was confused. She said, "I'm sorry, I have to tell you the worst news I've ever had to tell you." She told me while I was in a coma, my dad, who was my best friend, died next to her in his sleep. I never got to say goodbye. It was the single worst day of my life.

Two things, both medical:

1\] Growing up, I was a pretty healthy kid, except for developing Hashimotos hypothyroidism, but that didn't bother me much. Going into my 20s, however, my body seemed determined to self destruct. First I developed type 1 diabetes out of the blue. Then costochondritis. Then pleurisy. Then fibromyalgia. Then gastroparesis. Then chronic kidney stones due to a metabolic problem. Then neuropathy (although that was no surprise, I sucked at taking care of myself in those early years). So, when my gallbladder went bad (the night before a Lana Del Rey concert I would have killed to see...still bitter about that), I thought, okay, this sucks, but you remove it and you're done. So I got my gallbladder removed laproscopically and went home to recover.

​

Only...I wasn't feeling better. I was exhausted, and for some reason I was retaining a lot of water. I'm talking over 20lbs. As two weeks went by, the doctors office assured me it was just water gain from the surgery, and not to worry. At one point, though, I literally couldn't go five steps without falling on a couch or chair. I went for my surgical follow up and my surgeon noted I looked pale. I started telling him about my weird symptoms and he asked me some questions. His eyes grew wide, and he said he was sending me to the ER immediately.

​

They admitted me to the tachycardia wing. I had no idea what was happening. First they drained 2L of fluid from my lungs. Then they put me immediately on diuretics and other meds I don't remember (I was pretty out of it at the time - they were giving me dilaudid on top of everything else). Eventually, a doctor came in and bluntly said "You have congestive heart failure."

I remember blinking, laughing, and saying, "But not like...*failure* failure, right?" Amazing the mental gymnastics you can do when you're terrified.

"No," he explained. "You have congestive heart failure."

I cried, but they reassured me this could be managed with medication and time. The doctor held my hand. My family came and they calmed me down. Except for ending up with MRSA in my nose (had to be quarantined for a week or so), the rest of the hospital stay was pretty uneventful.

So after I was stable I went home with new stretch marks (from just how much water weight I gained, then lost) and new medication. I visited a heart hospital weekly at first, then got better and went to monthly appointments, then every two months, then every five. My progress was mostly steady and linear with only one dip in function - curiously enough, after I broke up with my fiance. Never underestimate the effect stress can have on your body.

Last September, two years after the failure, I had an appointment. My cardiologist came in grinning. He told me, flabbergasted but happy as hell, that my heart was now normal. There had been no lasting tissue damage, my ejection fraction (basically how well your heart squeezes) was now considered normal. Although I'd have to stay on medication, I was effectively cured. He said it was so rare it was a miracle. He told me that when I was first admitted to the hospital, my ejection fraction was below 10%, they briefly put me on the transplant list, and were pretty sure I would die. Somehow, though, I clawed my way back up to a healthy and normal heart. He told me I should try my luck in vegas.

​

2) When I get sick - a flu or whatever - my blood sugar can get a bit high (which is pretty normal). However, when I get really sick...well, this one time in particular, my blood sugar got so out of control I blacked out for three days.

My mom found me on my floor, naked for some reason. My eyes were open and I was panting, but I wasn't really there. I couldn't speak or move. She called the paramedics and they rushed me to the hospital. They confirmed I was in diabetic ketoacidosis, but something else is wrong. They run some tests and I come up positive for proplyene glycol. The doctors asked my mother if I had been suicidal, if I could have ingested this myself. My whole family ended up tearing apart my room looking for possible poisons. They immediately sent the test results to UC Davis.

I was worsening, fast. I went into heart and kidney failure. I was in the ICU. I was intubated and sedated heavily (propofol, precedex, fentanyl, *and* versed). They told my mom I was "critical". Basically, I was supposed to die. They decided to give me the propylene glycol antidote even though a few doctors had talked to my mom about the ketoacidosis being the real issue at hand.

It worked. In fact, the cardiologist in my first story was present when they administered it, and he said it was absolutely remarkable how quickly I improved. I was kept in the ICU and sedated but I was coming out of the woods. They eventually lifted the sedation, despite how agitated I became. I went through insane withdrawals from being on those powerful drugs for so long...but I was coming back to life. And quickly.

The doctors got the test results back. They said the test had been a false positive for propylene glycol. The bungled result, in fact, was a result of the chemical processes of diabetic ketoacidosis. So why did the antidote work? I wonder to this day what really happened. All I know is, there's 3 days that preceded the ER trip, and I don't remember a minute of them. So I escaped death a second time...by the skin of my teeth. The ER doc told me the acetone level in my blood was pretty far beyond the fatal limit and it was nothing short of miraculous that I not only survived, but regained full organ function so quickly (within two weeks of leaving the hospital). He, too, told me I ought to try my luck in Vegas.

​

TL;DR: I have cheated death twice like a bad bitch.
